title: Chrome for lawyers on Mac: PACER, CM/ECF, and research tips with Lazur in 2026
metaTitle: Chrome for Lawyers on Mac: PACER, Tabs and Lazur Help
description: Chrome for lawyers on Mac: set up profiles, tab groups, PACER fees and CM/ECF fixes. Then ask Lazur about any page out loud, in Chrome.
intro: Chrome for lawyers on Mac handles email, legal research, and court sites well. Three settings decide whether it stays out of your way: a current version, separate profiles, and PDF settings that stop filing errors. This page walks through each one. It also shows where Lazur helps while you work, and where it does not.
tldr: Check your Chrome version under More, Help, About Google Chrome. Chrome on Mac needs macOS 13 Ventura or later.
Keep firm and personal accounts in separate Chrome profiles.
If CM/ECF shows a Cannot redisplay error, set Chrome to download PDF files.
PACER charges $0.10 per page, and a single document costs at most $3.00 to access.
Lazur points, explains, and guides you one click at a time. It does not click for you.

blocks.text: Check your Chrome version and macOS first

Google's Chrome Enterprise release notes list Chrome 152 as the most recent stable entry. The stable date is September 1, 2026. Those notes do not separate Mac and Windows versions, so check your own copy. Open the three-dot More menu, select Help, then About Google Chrome. If a pending update exists, select Relaunch. If none exists, your browser is already current.

Chrome on Mac needs macOS 13 Ventura or later. Google's help page says it directly: 'To use Chrome on Mac, you need macOS 13 Ventura and up.' Chrome 150 is the last release that supports macOS 12. Check your system version under Apple menu > About This Mac. If you still run macOS 12 Monterey, Chrome updates stop at Chrome 150.

Google's release notes also say Chrome moves to a two-week release cycle starting with Chrome 153 in September 2026. The notes list that change under upcoming changes, and Google says plans might change. For a lawyer, the practical point is simple. Expect Chrome to update more often, and plan restarts around your calendar.

items: Relaunch reopens your tabs and windows on Mac.
Incognito windows do not come back after a relaunch. Save anything you need first.
Choose Not now, and the update applies the next time Chrome restarts.
If a filing deadline is close, file first, then relaunch.

blocks.text: Use separate Chrome profiles for firm and personal work

A Chrome profile keeps its own bookmarks, history, saved passwords, and signed-in accounts. Click the profile circle at the top right of the Chrome window to switch. Keep your firm Google account in one profile and your personal account in another. That stops firm files from mixing into a personal history.

Name each profile something plain, such as Firm and Personal. Chrome shows the name when you hover over the circle. Log in to PACER and CM/ECF from the profile your firm uses for filings. Use the personal profile for news, shopping, and anything with no client link. Switch profiles before you log in to anything.

items: Signing into a personal Google account in the firm profile, then saving client files there.
Keeping one profile for everything, so search history mixes personal and client work.
Filing from the wrong profile. Check the circle at the top right before you log in.

blocks.text: Chrome tab groups on Mac for matters and research

Lawyers open many tabs for one matter. A docket, a statute, a case page, a Google Scholar search, and a court rules page can all sit open at once. Chrome tab groups keep them together. Right-click a tab, add it to a group, then name the group and pick a color. A 2020 Google Blog post describes this flow, and groups are saved when Chrome closes and reopens. Menu labels can change between versions, so check the wording on your screen.

Use ⌘T for a new tab and ⌘W to close one. Press ⌘⇧T to reopen the tab you just closed. Press ⌘1 through ⌘8 to jump to a tab by its position, and ⌘9 for the last tab. Press Control and Tab to move to the next tab. Press ⌘L to jump to the address bar.

Name each group after the matter, not the day. A group called 'Motion' tells you nothing after a week. A group called 'Lee v. Harper, motion to dismiss' tells you everything. Keep research groups separate from filing groups, so you can close research tabs without touching a live docket.
Legal research in Chrome: where the time goes

The ABA's 2024 Legal Technology Survey Report found that legal research takes an average of 19% of lawyers' work hours. The survey ran from October to December 2024. The report summary says paid online legal research services are the format lawyers use most. Free online resources come second. 31% of respondents still report regularly using print materials.

That number shapes how you should set up Chrome. Much of your research will run through paid services, government sites, and free search pages. Give each source type its own group. Statutes, case law, and secondary sources need different tabs, and they often need different logins.

On a long opinion, ⌘F finds a word on the page. Press Return to step to the next match, and Shift Return to step back. Use the court's own wording in your search, such as 'motion to compel', because courts repeat their phrasing. Copy the citation before you close the tab.
PACER fees in Chrome: what you pay per page

PACER and CM/ECF run in the browser, and both carry fees. PACER charges $0.10 per page for access to case information. The cost to access a single document is capped at $3.00, which equals 30 pages. So a long document never costs more than $3.00 to open.

PACER also waives small bills. You owe no fee unless your usage in a quarter goes over $30. Charges of $30 or less in a quarter are waived. Once usage goes over $30, the charges apply. Look at the quarter total, not one search at a time.

Some secondary sources say PACER rates rise on January 1, 2027, with a higher per-page charge and a higher quarterly waiver. The official pricing FAQ does not say that. Check pacer.uscourts.gov before you budget for next year, and trust the court's page over any summary.

items: Read the case page before you open a long document.
Look at the page count first. The $3.00 cap still applies to each document.
Use the firm login, and log out when you finish, so charges go to the right account.
Track quarterly totals if you bill PACER costs to clients.

blocks.text: CM/ECF filing errors in Chrome and how to fix them

CM/ECF is the court filing system behind many filing links. Most problems in Chrome come from three things. A PDF opens inside Chrome in a way the court's system does not like. A page goes stale. Old cookies or cached files get in the way. Each has a simple fix once you know which one you have.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida issued a notice dated October 23, 2020. It said Chrome's PDF plug-in can cause a 'Cannot redisplay' error when you open a document from a Notice of Electronic Filing link. The court's workaround is to set Chrome to download PDFs, or to use another browser.

Open Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings > Additional content settings > PDF documents. Choose the option to download PDF files instead of opening them in Chrome. Menu labels shift between versions, so look for the PDF setting under site settings if the names differ. Then test one document before a deadline, because that notice is from 2020.

If the filing option does not show, refresh the page. PACER's NextGen guidance says to refresh with F5, then clear cookies, cache, and history if the menu still does not appear. On a Mac keyboard, press ⌘R to refresh. Then open Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Clear browsing data, or press ⌘⇧⌫.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California says its CM/ECF system was tested with Firefox and Internet Explorer, but not with Chrome or Safari. That page may be dated, so treat it as a warning, not a ruling. It also advises clearing the browser cache when the Civil e-filing option is missing after you log in to PACER.

items: Check the profile circle and confirm you are in the firm profile.
Set Chrome to download PDF files, then test one document.
Log in to PACER, then open the case.
If the filing option is missing, press ⌘R, then clear cache and cookies.
Save the confirmation page to the matter folder before you close the tab.

blocks.text: Common mistakes lawyers make in Chrome on Mac

items: Filing from an incognito window. Incognito windows do not come back after a relaunch.
Putting off the update until a deadline week, then relaunching in a hurry.
Staying on macOS 12. Chrome 151 and later need macOS 13 or later.
Saving firm documents through a personal Google account.
Trusting an old court notice as current. Check the date before you act on it.

blocks.text: Most of these fixes take a few minutes. The worst time to find them is the evening of a deadline. Do the version check and the PDF setting on an ordinary afternoon. Then you will not need them in a hurry.
A filing afternoon in Chrome with Lazur

Here is a realistic run through the steps above, with Lazur helping you find each control. You still make every click and every filing decision. Hold ⌥ ⌘ for each question, and hold fn when you want dictation.

items: Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask, 'Which profile am I in?' Lazur points at the profile circle and answers out loud.
Ask, 'Where is the PDF download setting?' Lazur circles the setting and labels it. You make the change.
Ask, 'Walk me through clearing browsing data.' Lazur guides one click at a time and waits for each click.
Hold fn and dictate a short cover note. The clean text lands at your cursor.
Ask Lazur to add a reminder in Apple Reminders to check the docket next week.

blocks.text: Where Lazur helps in Chrome, and where it stops

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘, which is Option and Command together, and ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. It points at things, explains them, and guides you one click at a time.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for Chrome or any other app. That matters for a filing. You make each click, so you know exactly what went into the record.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. That helps with a client email, a note, or a first draft of a cover letter. Lazur also drafts text for you to review. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans.

Research requests run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension. When the job finishes, Lazur returns a summary and a report. You still check the sources before you rely on any finding.

Privacy matters more for lawyers than for most users. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm still sets its own rules for privileged material, so follow them before you ask about a client file.
Lazur pricing and the trial in Chrome

Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Pro costs $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, and includes 250 AI actions. Power costs $120 a month, or $96 a month billed annually, and includes 1,000 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both plans.

Test the trial on a real matter. Ask about a PACER fee page, a docket, and a dense order. Note how often you reach for it. Then decide whether Pro or Power fits your month. Check [current plan details](/pricing) before you commit.

faq.question: Is Chrome a good browser for lawyers on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes, for email, legal research sites, and PACER. Most problems come from three areas: an old version, a PDF setting that blocks filing, and a stale cache. Fix those and Chrome works well for daily court and research work.

faq.question: Which Chrome and macOS versions do I need on a Mac?
faq.answer: Chrome on Mac needs macOS 13 Ventura or later. Google's release notes list Chrome 152 as the latest stable entry, with a stable date of September 1, 2026. Check your own version under More, then Help, then About Google Chrome.

faq.question: Why does CM/ECF show a Cannot redisplay error in Chrome?
faq.answer: A 2020 notice from the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida says Chrome's PDF plug-in can cause that error. Set Chrome to download PDF files, then open the document again. Test the fix before a deadline.

faq.question: How much does PACER cost per page?
faq.answer: PACER charges $0.10 per page for access to case information. Access to a single document is capped at $3.00, which equals 30 pages. Charges of $30 or less in a quarter are waived.

faq.question: Will Lazur file documents for me in Chrome?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It points at things, explains them, guides you one click at a time, and drafts text. You make each filing decision and each click.

faq.question: Does Lazur store what I ask about a client file?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Follow your firm's rules for privileged material.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: Can I try Lazur before I pay?
faq.answer: Yes. The Pro trial lasts 3 days and needs no credit card. It starts when you first open the app. After the trial, Pro costs $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually.
